verdicts.explanation: The paper's own AIMD gives room-temperature-extrapolated 7.9 ± 3.7 mS/cm and EA = 249 ± 18 meV for the reference Li7P3S11 structure, so the record matches and the computational origin is correct.

The paper states that for LiBH4 the room-temperature-extrapolated conductivity from its AIMD is 0.44 ± 0.30 mS/cm, and the record's null activation energy is acceptable since the quoted sentence does not give one.
The paper reports an additional AIMD run for LiB3H8 at 363 K giving 82 ± 23 mS/cm, excluded from the Arrhenius fit, so the record's null activation energy is correct and the origin is computational.

The paper says the Li10Ge(PSe6)2 structure was simulated in Ref. [68] and that its reported EA of 190 ± 40 meV and room-temperature conductivity of 24 mS/cm come from there, so literature_cited is correct and 0.19 eV is the same value in eV.

The paper states EA = 295 meV and σ = 8.3 mS/cm for the most pure phase Li7P3S11 sample in Ref. [71], and gives no measurement temperature, so the null temperature is correct and the origin is literature_cited.

The quoted sentence gives 3.2 mS/cm and EA = 124 meV only as 'in Ref. [72]' and never names the material; the Li2S-P2S5 glass-ceramic identity is inferred from the reference title, which is too weak a basis under the strict standard.

The paper says an orthorhombic distortion of the Li(BH)6 structure was found to have conductivity of up to 0.1 S/cm at 700 K [76], which matches the record's value, unit, temperature and literature_cited origin.

The paper states that hexagonal LiBH4 has been found experimentally to have an ionic conductivity of the order of 1 mS/cm at 383 K, citing [73-75], so the record's value, temperature and literature_cited origin are correct.
